<x_0.0674><y_0.075>Mr Lemeri hath thewn, that excrement is not the only 
matter capable of producing this phofphorus with alum; 
but that, on the contrary, almost all animal and even ve-
getable matters are fit for this combination; that though 
Mr Homberg mixed alum in equal quantities only with 
the fecal matter, it may be ufed in a much greater pro-
portion; and, in certain cafes, will fucceed the better; 
that, according to the nature of the fulbiances to be 
worked on, the quantity of that felt may be more or leis 
increafed; and that whatever is added, more than the 
dole requihte for each matter, ferver only to leften the 
virtue of the photophorus, or even destroys it entirely; 
that the degree of fire applied null be different according 
to the nature of those matters; and, latily, that falls 
containing exactly the fame acid with that of alum, or 
the acid of thofe fals separated from its baffs and reduced 
into spirit, do not anfwer in the prefent operation : which 
thews, fays Mr Lemeri, that many fulphureous matters 
may be fubllituted for excrement in this operation; but 
that there are no false, or very few, if any, that will 
fucceed in the place of alum.<x_0.9756><y_0.3906><class_Text>

<x_0.0693><y_0.3898>This phofphorus, made either by Mr Homberg's or 
by Mr Lemeri’s method, finnes both by day and by 
night. Belides emitting light, it takes fire foon after it 
is exposed to the air, and kindles all combultible matters 
with which it comes in contact; and this without being 
rubbed or heated.<x_0.9766><y_0.4797><class_Text>

<x_0.0703><y_0.4805>Meff. Homberg and Lemeri have given the moft probable and the moft natural explanation of the caule of 
the accention and other phenomena of this phofphorus. 
What they lay amounts in short to what follows.<x_0.9775><y_0.5406><class_Text>

<x_0.0713><y_0.5414>Alum is known to be a neutral fatt, confiling of the 
vitriolic acid and a calcareous earth. When this fatt is 
calcined with the fecal matter, or other fulbances a bounding in oil, the volatile principles of thefe fulbances, 
fuch as their phlegn, their fats, and their oils, exhale 
in the fame manner as if they were difficilled; and there 
is nothing left in the matras, when thofe principles are 
dilipated, but a charred matter, like that which is found 
in retorts wherein fuch mixts have been decompoiled by 
difficiliation.<x_0.9785><y_0.6891><class_Text>

<x_0.0723><y_0.6898>This remainder therefore is nothing but a mixture of 
alum and charcoal. Now, as the acid of this fatt, which 
is the vitriolic, hath a greater affinity with the phlogilton 
than with any other fulblance, it will quit its balls to 
unit with the phlogilton of the coal, and be converted 
by that union into a fulphur. And this is the very cafe, 
of which we have certain proofs in the operation for pre-
pating this phofphorus; for when, after the volatile 
principles of the oily matter are drawn off, the fire is 
increased, in order to combine closely together the fixed 
parts that remain in the matras, that is, the alum and 
the charred matter, we perceive at the mouth of the ma-
tras a final blue fulphoreous flame, and a pungent fmell 
of burning fulphur. Nay, when the operation is finish-<x_0.9795><y_0.9031><class_Text>
